claims.text: The transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition is driven by temperature-dependent evolution of local chemical order within the B2 phase.
Local chemical order in the B2 phase modulates the critical resolved shear stress for dislocation slip in ordered domains.
The transition is not caused by grain-boundary embrittlement.
The initial material contains a disordered FCC matrix and an ordered B2 phase.
The initial phase boundaries have a fine lamellar or cellular morphology.
Grain-boundary segregation is thermodynamically unfavorable or kinetically negligible under the proposed aging conditions.
Grain coarsening is minimal under the proposed aging conditions.
Evolution of short-range or local chemical order in B2 modifies phase-boundary coherency and interfacial energy.
Intermediate-temperature aging forms B2-to-DO3 order or complex short-range-order clusters within the B2 phase.
The proposed local chemical orders increase lattice friction or Peierls stress.
The proposed local chemical orders increase the energy barrier for superlattice intrinsic stacking-fault formation.
Increased ordering changes dislocation behavior from planar easy glide to cross-slip or dislocation locking.
Cross-slip or dislocation locking causes brittle fracture at intermediate aging temperatures.
At higher temperatures, the local chemical orders dissolve or reorganize into a less slip-resistant configuration.
Dissolution or reorganization of local chemical order restores planar slip and ductility.
Phase boundaries amplify embrittlement by restricting dislocation motion across the FCC/B2 interface.
Yield strength peaks and ductility drops at the temperature of maximum B2 local chemical order.
Ductility recovers at higher temperatures as local chemical order dissolves.
Fracture in the brittle state occurs by transgranular cleavage or along phase boundaries without detectable impurity segregation.
The embrittlement regime is defined by a local-ordering parameter greater than 0.5 while grain-boundary energy remains unchanged.
